title: Dedaun Rimba: the first chapter of Kwasa Damansara.
videoTitle: PROPERTY REVIEW #469 | DEDAUN RIMBA, KWASA DAMANSARA
excerpt: The first completed homes in a long-hyped master plan arrive with the roads, parks and MRT already finished — and with the compromises a townhouse always carries.
takeaways: The first completed homes in Kwasa Damansara, built after the roads, parks and MRT.
Strata landed homes arranged around a central park, with no back lanes.
No shops yet, some puzzling details and rising competition are the concerns.

sections.heading: What sets it apart
paragraphs: Dedaun Rimba is the first completed project in Kwasa Damansara: about 264 leasehold strata homes, with link houses around a central park and an outer ring of townhouses. The rows are single-loaded, so homes face the garden and there are no back lanes.

The 1,396 sq ft lower townhouse reverses the usual layout, with the kitchen at the front and the living room opening onto the garden, plus a ground-floor bedroom, three bathrooms and two tandem parking bays. The owner paid about RM780,000.

sections.heading: Where it is
paragraphs: Kwasa Damansara's roads, parks and MRT station were finished before the homes; the owner commutes by MRT, which you can hear from the garden. For now, residents rely on neighbouring Kota Damansara for shops.

sections.heading: Rent and returns
paragraphs: It is too new for rents to be known, and most early buyers appear to be moving in themselves. Prices are already moving: garden-facing link houses sold at about RM1.38 million are being offered on the subsale market at about RM1.9 million.

standout.title: Homes that face a shared garden
standout.body: Instead of back lanes, the link houses ring a central park, and each home's best spaces open onto it rather than the street. Because it is strata, with guarded security and a management that keeps the facades uniform, the garden works as an extension of every home.

pros: A master plan that built the infrastructure first: roads, walkways, parks, street lighting and an operating MRT station, with the master developer's own headquarters up before land was parcelled out to other developers.
Strata landed living: maintained common areas and facades, homes that open onto a central park, managed parking, and deliberately simple, low-maintenance facilities.
The developer's design flair: subtle wall textures, angled columns, a Santorini-toned pool and careful partitions, which is why many buyers trust the brand.
cons: The township will take years: there are no shops yet, so families rely on Kota Damansara, and prices already match similar condo layouts.
Puzzling details: feeder pillars painted green rather than screened with planting, lower townhouses whose living rooms open straight onto a shared walkway, and outer units facing very wide roads.
Competition: Sunsuria, MRCB, YTL and others are building here, which matters most for high-rise buyers, and the area's appeal rests on the MRT and the new roads.

closing: Sean's punchline: strata landed homes from a reputable developer, under RM800,000 in the Klang Valley and within walking distance of a park and an MRT station, are now rare.
sourceNote: Based on Sean's full English captions for this September 2026 episode. The 3 on 3 follows the three things he likes and the three concerns he names, in his order, at the end of the video. A viewer who bought a unit let Sean view it.
